text: The Script Debugger is a real, standard debugging tool built directly into the platform for the server-side JavaScript engine from Chapter 2. It works the same way any debugger in any IDE works: flag a line, trigger the script, and execution freezes right there so you can look around before letting it continue.

A breakpoint is a flag on a specific line — here, the line assigning newPriority inside a before-update Business Rule on incident. Once that breakpoint is set, updating an Incident that fires this rule pauses the transaction the instant execution reaches that line, instead of running straight through.

Once paused, the debugger gives you the same vocabulary as any IDE debugger. Step over runs the current line and moves to the next one. Step into follows execution inside a function that line calls. Step out returns you to whatever called the current function. These are standard debugging controls, just pointed at a Business Rule instead of a standalone app.

The real value of pausing is what you can see. With the breakpoint hit, you can inspect current and previous directly, check the local variable newPriority itself, and see the call stack — exactly which rule, which function, called into the next. That's the core debugging move: stop guessing what a variable holds, and look at it directly.

The Script Debugger's real limit is synchronous, session-attached execution. It can't help with a Business Rule configured to run asynchronously, queued outside your session. It can't help with a Scheduled Job running in the background with no session attached. And it obviously can't help with Client Scripts, since those run as real JavaScript in the browser, not on the server at all.

The Script Debugger is the right first tool for a synchronous server-side problem, and the wrong tool the moment a script runs async or in the background. Next lesson: gs.info and the System Log, the tool that works exactly when the debugger can't attach.
